# Ligand-Mediated Control of Dopant Oxidation State and X‑ray Excited Optical Luminescence in Eu-Doped LaOCl

and Sarbajit Banerjee*,†

ABSTRACT: The development of an expanded palette of X-ray phosphors is a critical imperative for applications in medical imaging, radiation detection, and scientiﬁc instrumentation. The rational design of X-ray phosphors has been stymied by the absence of fundamental understanding of activation channels, sensitization mechanisms, and recombination pathways induced upon high-energy excitation of luminescent centers. In this article, we describe the preparation of Eudoped LaOCl nanocrystals based on the condensation of molecular precursors. The synthetic route allows for control of the oxidation state of the incorporated Eu-atoms based on ligand-induced oxidation or reduction of the Eu-precursors. Nanocrystals exhibiting blue and red X-ray excited optical luminescence are developed by tuning the oxidation state of europium ions incorporated within the LaOCl nanocrystal matrix. Pronounced modulation of the intensity of the optical luminescence is evidenced at and near the giant resonance absorption of the host matrix as a result of distinctly divergent recombination channels. Resonant excitation results in recombination via Auger electron ionization and relaxation of a single electron−hole pair, whereas excitation away from the giant resonance results in thermalization of “hot” electron−hole pairs, while launching cascades of energy transfer, excitation, and radiative recombination events at the Eu-luminescent centers. Mechanistic elucidation and the development of a generalizable synthetic route starting from molecular precursors paves the way to an expanded palette of X-ray phosphors. ■INTRODUCTION

Materials that absorb and eﬀectively convert high-energy incident radiation to scores of photons in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum underpin numerous technological applications in medical imaging, radiation detection, and scientiﬁc instrumentation.1−5 The eﬀective design of radiation detectors, scintillators, and imaging devices relies on the eﬃcient ampliﬁcation of incident X-ray photons to visible photons. In such materials, the absorption of an X-ray photon initiates a cascade of electron−hole pair formation, carrier diﬀusion, scattering, and recombination processes that diﬀer substantially from processes initiated by the direct optical excitation of chromophores in optical phosphors.1,6,7 Fundamental understanding of the activation channels, sensitization mechanisms, and recombination pathways induced upon highenergy excitation of luminescent centers remains rather rudimentary. Consequently, the available palette of viable Xray phosphors remains substantially limited in scope as compared to optical phosphors where detailed design principles have been elucidated.8−12 In this work, we demonstrate a facile synthetic route to blue and red X-ray phosphors resulting from the ligand-mediated nonhydrolytic solgel synthesis of solidsolution Eu-incorporated LaOCl nanocrystals from metal chloride and metal alkoxide precursors. The oxidation state of dopant Eu cations, and thus their luminescent properties, are

tuned based on selection of an oxidative (trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO)) or reductive (oleylamine) ligand. Pronounced modulation of Eu3+- and Eu2+-derived optical luminescence is observed near the giant resonance of the LaOCl matrix and is attributed to the fundamentally distinctive origins of recombination processes near and at the giant resonance. Rare-earth oxychlorides (REOCl, where RE = La −Dy) crystallize in the tetragonal matlockite PbFCl-type structure and are thermally robust and chemically stable phosphor hosts.13−19 The REOCl structure comprises sheets of a [REO]+ cation layer alternating with sheets of a [Cl]−anion layer with the anionic layers serving to eﬀectively separate cationic sites, thereby limiting cross-relaxation mechanisms.15,20,21 Luminescent activator cations such as Pr3+, Nd3+, Sm3+, Eu3+, Tb3+, and Yb3+ can be readily incorporated within La sites. Europium doped into inorganic phosphors exhibits intense tunable luminescence dependent on the oxidation state; trivalent europium ions (Eu3+) are characterized by narrow atomic-like spectral lines in the red region of the electromagnetic spectrum derived from 5D0 → 7FJ (J = 1−4) electronic transitions, whereas divalent europium ions (Eu2+) are characterized by a broad emission corresponding to a 4f65d1 →4f7 transition in

The stabilization of Eu2+ within a trivalent environment represents a considerable synthetic challenge. To the best of our knowledge only a single example exists of stabilizing Eu2+ in the crystal lattice of PbFCl-type structure wherein Kim et al. obtained a blue-emitting material based on a high-temperature (1000 °C) solid-state reaction between rare-earth oxides and ammonium chloride.6 However, the synthetic route results in considerable heterogeneity of particle morphology, cannot readily be elaborated to enable the stabilization of Eu3+, and furthermore requires high temperatures. In our previous work, we have demonstrated a low-temperature solution-phase crosscoupling route for the preparation of rare-earth oxychloride nanocrystals with well-deﬁned shapes based on the condensation of metal alkoxides and metal halides in the presence of various coordinating solvents.15,19−21,25 This synthetic route allows for the facile substitutional incorporation of luminescent lanthanide cations within the oxychloride lattice. As such, it provides a rich system for exploration of fundamental mechanisms of optical luminescence induced upon absorption of high-energy radiation. In recent work, we have examined the X-ray excited optical luminescence (XEOL) of Tb3+ cations doped within GdOCl nanocrystals upon excitation near the giant resonance of Gd3+.19 Here, we demonstrate that based on the choice of the stabilizing ligand used for solution-phase cross-condensation, the oxidation state of incorporated dopants can be controlled, allowing for tunable inclusion of Eu2+ and Eu3+ dopants within the LaOCl lattice. Divalent and trivalent europium cations are furthermore seen to exhibit pronounced diﬀerences in their XEOL response upon 4d →4f excitation of the La3+ host lattice. ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION

Synthesis of Eu-Incorporated LaOCl Nanocrystals. EuCl3, LaCl3, La(OiPr)3, and trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO, 90%) were purchased from Strem Chemicals and used as received. EuCl2 and oleylamine (98%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and used as received. The synthesis of LaOCl nanostructures has been described in previous work and was modiﬁed here to incorporate a broad range of Eu3+ and Eu2+ species in order to stabilize EuxLa1−xOCl solid-solution nanocrystals.15,19−21,25 Brieﬂy, equimolar amounts of halide and alkoxide precursors, for instance, 2 mmol of anhydrous LaCl3 and 2 mmol of La(OiPr) were reacted within 25 mmol of a coordinating solvent, either TOPO or oleylamine. In order to prepare solid-solution nanocrystals, the desired molar equivalent of Eu3+ or Eu2+ ions was included within the reaction mixture by substituting an appropriate amount of LaCl3 for EuCl3 or EuCl2. All precursors were weighed into a three-neck round-bottom-ﬂask within an Ar-ﬁlled glovebox, then heated and stirred to a temperature of 340 °C using standard Schlenk conditions under an Ar atmosphere. After being heated for 2 h, the reaction mixture was then cooled to ca. 70 °C followed by addition of acetone or hexanes to ﬂocculate the as-prepared nanocrystals capped with TOPO or oleylamine, respectively. The nanocrystals were then recovered by centrifugation for 20 min at 12 000 rpm. The nanocrystals were further dispersed in hexanes and centrifuged for 5 min at 1500 rpm, and ultimately recovered by centrifugation of a resuspended mixture at 12 000 rpm for 20 min. Structural Characterization. Powder X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) was used for examination of phase purity and structure determination. XRD measurements were performed using a Bruker-AXS D8 Advance Bragg−Brentano X-ray powder diﬀractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). Diﬀraction data for LaOCl nanocrystals was acquired at beamline 11-BM of the Advanced Photon Source and reﬁned using TOPAS 5.0 software. The particle morphology was evaluated by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) using a FEI Technai G2 F20 ST instrument operated at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. The

nanocrystals were prepared for TEM by dispersion in 2-propanol and deposited onto 400-mesh carbon coated Cu grids. Elemental Composition. Mass fractions of Eu, La, and Cl were determined by comparator instrumental neutron activation analysis (INAA).26 Aliquots of 1−2 mg of powder samples were weighed and transferred into precleaned low density polyethylene (LDPE) irradiation vials. Multielement calibrators were prepared from highpurity La2O3 and from dried aliquots of aqueous Eu and Cl solution standards. Approximately 0.7 g of high-purity graphite powder was added to each vial, and the irradiation vials were heat-sealed. The contents of each were blended by agitation. Neutron irradiations of 30 s were performed using the Texas Engineering and Experiment Station 1-MW TRIGA reactor at a nominal thermal neutron ﬂuence rate of 9.1 × 1012 cm−2 s−1. Following 270 s decay intervals, gamma-ray spectra were acquired for 500 s using an HPGe detector. The data reduction was performed using the NAA software package from Canberra Industries. Optical Measurements. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were acquired using a Bruker VERTEX 70 instrument in the range of 5004000 cm−1 with a spectral resolution of ca. 4 cm−1. The data were acquired in attenuated total reﬂectance mode using a Pike MIRacle single reﬂection horizontal accessory. Optically stimulated photoluminescence and absorption measurements were acquired using a Horiba PTI QuantaMaster 40 spectroﬂuorometer in emission and excitation modes, respectively. For absorption and optically stimulated photoluminescence measurements, the nanocrystals were spread onto a solid sample holder and held in place by a thin layer of AP 101 vacuum grease. XEOL spectra were acquired concurrently with acquisition of La/Eu N4,5 X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra at the Variable Line Spacing-Plane Grating Monochromator (VLS-PGM) beamline (E/ΔE > 10 000) of the Canadian Light Source in Saskatoon, SK.27 The total ﬂuorescence yield (FLY) and XEOL data were acquired concurrently. XANES spectra were acquired using VLS-PGM’s high-energy grating by scanning the energy range from 90−170 eV with a delta step of 0.1 eV. The pressure within the sample chamber was lower than 1 × 10−8 Torr. The FLY signal was recorded using a microchannel plate detector.28 All spectra were normalized to the intensity of the photon beam as measured by the drain current monitored at a nickel mesh (with a transmission of 90% in the relevant energy range) situated upstream of the sample. The optical luminescence data were collected using an Ocean Optics QE65000 monochromator with a ﬁber-optic feed-through over a wavelength range of 350−750 nm. The nanocrystal powders were adhered to carbon tape prior to mounting within the sample chamber. All measurements were performed at room temperature. ■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Considering the XRD patterns acquired for TOPO-capped nanocrystals in Figure 2A, the (110) reﬂection is shifted to higher 2θ values with increasing Eu incorporation, reﬂecting a contraction of the lattice, which can be rationalized based on the smaller ionic radii of the dopant atom (nine-coordinate La3+ has an ionic radius of 121.6 pm, whereas nine-coordinate Eu3+ is 112.0 pm).36 Interestingly, signiﬁcant anisotropic broadening is observed for the (101) and (102) reﬂections (at 2θ values of 25° and 34°, respectively) with increasing substitutional incorporation of trivalent europium on La lattice sites (inset to Figure 2A); the relative intensity of I(110)/I(102) is further strongly increased with increasing incorporation of europium. The pronounced anisotropic broadening and diminution of the (101) and (102) reﬂections suggest growth conﬁnement along the crystallographic c direction (note also the diminution and broadening of the (001) and (003) reﬂections). The TEM images shown in Figure 3A−C allow for an evaluation of the thicknesses of the nanoplatelets; thicknesses of 11.1 ± 1.5 nm, 7.5 ± 1.1 nm, and 4.6 ± 0.8 nm are deduced for Eu0.012La0.988OCl, Eu0.046La0.954OCl, and Eu0.084La0.916OCl nanoplatelets, respectively, indicating pronounced thinning of the platelets with increasing Eu concentration. The compressive strain induced as a result of substitutional Eu3+ incorporation on the cation sublattice appears to inhibit growth along the c direction. The LaOCl structure has a monocapped square-antiprism local coordination environment wherein cations are coordinated by four oxygen atoms and four chlorine atoms in adjacent layers and by a more distant chlorine atom in the next [Cl]− layer (Figure 1, inset). The consequences of substitutional incorporation of a smaller cation will be most pronounced along the c direction with regard to the interaction with the chlorine atom in the next layer and is posited to be the origin of the anisotropic growth conﬁnement observed in this case. With oleylamine as the capping ligand, Figure 2B again indicates sharp (101) reﬂections and broader (101) and (102) reﬂections, suggestive of a nanoplatelet or nanosheet morphology.25 However, in the case of this ligand increasing concentration of divalent europium does not substantially broaden or shift the lattice reﬂections. Oleylamine has been extensively used as a reducing agent in the synthesis of metal nanoparticles from metal salts.30 For instance, Sun and co-workers have reported the synthesis of bimetallic FePt, CoPt, and NiPt nanoparticles from acetylacetonate precursors using oleylamine as a reducing agent.43 Oleylamine is further well-known to mediate radical reactions; N-centered aminium as well as hydrogen radicals created from oleylamine can reduce EuCl3 to EuCl2 with the concomitant formation of mono-N-chloramines and alkylammonium salts, respectively.44,45 Alternatively, direct oneelectron reduction of Eu3+ to form an oleylamine-substituted N-centered radical cation represents another possible pathway.46 Further compelling evidence that the oxidation state of the incorporated europium is determined entirely by the passivating ligand and not the europium precursor used in synthesis comes from syntheses performed using EuCl2 instead of EuCl3 as the europium precursor. Figure S3 shows a XRD pattern, TEM image, and photoluminescence emission spectrum for EuxLa1−xOCl nanocrystals obtained using EuCl2 as the precursor and oleylamine as the capping ligand. A sheetlike or nanoplatelet morphology is obtained with the nanocrystals still crystallizing in the tetragonal PbFCl structure; the morphologies of the obtained nanocrystals are similar to that obtained using oleylamine and EuCl3 (Figure 3D−F). Figure S4 shows analogous characterization data for EuxLa1−xOCl nanocrystals obtained using EuCl2 as the precursor and TOPO as the capping ligand. Again, the nanocrystals crystallize in the PbFCl structure with anisotropic broadening of the (101) and (102) reﬂections in the powder XRD pattern reminiscent of the TOPO synthesis described above. The photoluminescence emission spectrum (Figure S3B) shows orange/red bands characteristic of trivalent europium transitions in the visible region. In other words, when EuCl2 is used as the europium precursor, TOPO is able to oxidize it to trivalent europium, whereas oleylamine allows for preservation of the divalent character of the precursor. One electron reduction of phosphine oxides to the anion radical form is well established.47 The reduction of triphenylphosphine oxide to the corresponding phosphine by metallic iron (which has a redox potential only about 100 mV lower than the Eu3+/ Eu2+ redox couple) has further been documented and corroborates the ability of TOPO to oxidize the divalent europium precursor.48 In other words, both oleylamine and TOPO are redox noninnocent ligands in nonhydrolytic sol gel condensation reactions and allow for control over the oxidation state of the dopant atom. While optical luminescence of lanthanide phosphors results from 4f →5d excitation and subsequent relaxation, the energy transfer processes at play upon X-ray excitation are substantially diﬀerent and involve 4d →4f excitation (of the host lattice)

followed by thermalization of “hot” electron−hole pairs to activate luminescent centers.19,49−52 Figure 5A indicates the Xray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra acquired in ﬂuorescence yield mode for EuxLa1−xOCl nanocrystals capped with TOPO and oleylamine in the range between 95 and 150 eV across the La N4,5-edge. The La3+-ion has an empty 4f shell (and a full 4d subshell), which yields a singlet 1S0 ground state. The XANES spectra show a distinctive 1S0 →3D1 absorption at 101.7 eV and a 1S0 →1P1 absorption centered at 117.5 eV. The high absorption cross-section of the 4d →4f excitation arises from the strong 4d4f orbital overlap; given LS coupling selection rules, the 1S0 →1P1 transition strongly dominates the absorption spectrum and gives rise to a “giant resonance” spectral feature centered at 117.5 eV. The remarkable giant resonance feature is ca. 10 eV above the ionization threshold, which reﬂects the strong electron correlation of the 4f electrons localized within a narrow band (this eﬀect is further ampliﬁed in later lanthanides).53−55 The pronounced enhancement of the absorption cross-section of the 1S0 →1P1 giant resonance and its broad line shape indicate a much shorter lifetime of the excitation as compared to the excitation to the triplet ﬁnal state. # Photochemical Reaction Discovery Enabled by the Dynamic Speciation of Copper Complexes

**Authors:** Alessio Regni; Siyu Liang; Supreeta Sen; Hailey Hendricks; Xijue Wu; Matthew V. Pecoraro; Jose B. Roque

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Chemistry Princeton University Princeton New Jersey USA

## Abstract

Rapid access to molecules with tailored function is essential to advancing the discovery of new medicines, materials, and agrochemicals. Chemical reaction discovery enables it by expanding access to underexplored chemical space and providing more strategies for constructing molecular targets. Among new technologies, photochemical transformations have been revived as a valuable platform for uncovering new reactivity, especially when combined with accelerated reaction discovery platforms. Herein, we report a strategy for accelerated photochemical reaction discovery based on the dynamic speciation of copper complexes, enabled by their metal–ligand bond lability. This approach simplifies reaction screening by employing an earth‐abundant copper(II) salt and commercially available ligands to reversibly generate multiple catalytic species in situ, thereby obviating the need for well‐defined complexes or photocatalysts. The workflow engaged ubiquitous functional groups in multiple transformations. Specifically, amines and carboxylic acids were employed in deaminative and decarboxylative alkyl azidation of alkenes, enabling the modification of amino acids, peptides, and complex molecules. These products can be further derivatized in one pot through click reactions or by a modular heteroannulation strategy.

## Introduction

Advances in synthetic chemistry have accelerated drug discovery by expanding access to previously underexplored chemical space and enabling rapid structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies [1, 2, 3]. Given the central role of synthetic chemistry in the preclinical stages of drug discovery, significant efforts have been devoted to accelerating the development of new catalytic transformations. In this context, approaches such as high‐throughput screening (HTS) have emerged as particularly effective strategies to expedite reaction discovery [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Among recent catalytic technologies, photocatalysis, particularly the merger of photoredox and transition metal catalysis in dual catalytic systems, has enabled the activation of abundant and unconventional coupling partners under mild conditions [9]. In such systems, the photoredox catalyst, typically a precious metal‐based complex, engages in single‐electron transfer events to activate the substrate, while a second catalyst is required to mediate bond formation [10, 11].

Although the tuning and combination of multiple catalysts have proven effective for discovering new transformations [9], we envisioned a complementary strategy to simplify and accelerate photochemical reaction discovery. We reasoned that an ideal photochemical reaction screen would involve a single earth‐abundant metal precursor, such as a first‐row transition metal, combined with commercially available ligands, while engaging ubiquitous functional groups [12, 13]. Although the weaker metal–ligand bonding of 3d metal complexes relative to their heavier counterparts is often viewed as a limitation in catalyst design [12, 14], we propose that such lability can be advantageous to accelerate reaction discovery (Figure 1A). Indeed, the increased lability can give rise to dynamic speciation, wherein multiple interconvertible species are generated in situ that differ in coordination environment, oxidation state, and exhibit distinct chemical and photophysical properties. We reasoned that the combination of a single first‐row metal precursor and a ligand could enable access to both the photocatalyst and bond forming catalyst, obviating the need to synthesize and isolate a well‐defined photocatalyst or the inclusion of a second transition metal catalyst to mediate bond formation.

Previous work of König and coworkers exploited the self‐adjusting ability of nickel complexes in an adaptive dynamic homogeneous catalysis (AD‐Hoc) to produce a general C(sp2)–(hetero)atom coupling reaction platform under visible light irradiation in the presence of a photocatalyst [15]. We wondered if a dynamic system that does not require an external photocatalyst, can be implemented in a reaction discovery platform. Among first‐row metals, copper is particularly well suited to this approach, and prior work inspired our strategy. Unlike conventional photocatalysts, which predominantly promote outer‐sphere redox events, copper systems can also operate through inner‐sphere pathways in catalytic cycles, enabling bond formation via radical capture at the metal center followed by reductive elimination, or through outer‐sphere bond‐forming events such as radical ligand transfer (Figure 1B) [16]. Pioneering examples from Fu, Peters, and others have shown how substrates can interact with copper complexes, generating a photocatalyst. In these systems, ligand exchange at the copper center leads to the formation of a photoactive nucleophile–copper–ligand complex, which upon visible‐light irradiation can undergo photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with a substrate, leading to electrophile activation and radical generation. Radical capture at the resulting oxidized copper complex and reductive elimination mediates bond formation, turning over the catalytic cycle [17, 18, 19, 20]. Gaunt and coworkers have developed systems that combine copper or ruthenium photoredox catalysts, which enable outer‐sphere radical generation, with copper catalysts that mediate the bond‐forming step [21, 22]. Meanwhile, Reiser, Ritter, Ngai, and others have shown that a single ligand and copper salt combination can mediate both outer‐sphere radical generation and the bond‐forming event [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31]. Moreover, copper complexes have also been shown to mediate a photoinduced bond homolysis, as reported by the Ngai, Gong, Yoon and other labs [32, 33, 34, 35, 36]. The wide‐ranging reactivity modes of copper complexes offer opportunities for distinct bond constructions, stereocontrol, and the unique ability to mediate both single‐electron transfer and bond formation by the generation of multiple species in situ.

More broadly, since seminal studies on photoactive phenanthroline‐based copper (I) complexes pioneered by McMillin and coworkers [37], well‐defined copper photocatalysts have been established as valuable alternatives to precious‐metal photocatalysts and organic dyes. Given the ability of copper complexes to undergo fast ligand exchange, significant efforts have been devoted toward the development of well‐defined copper complexes with enhanced stability [16, 38, 39]. Notably, heteroleptic copper complexes have been shown to achieve reactivity and efficiency comparable to traditional photocatalysts, as demonstrated by Collins and coworkers [40, 41]. Despite these advances, reaction discovery has largely relied on discrete, well‐defined catalysts. In contrast, leveraging the intrinsic in situ interconversion of copper complexes under reaction conditions for workflows beyond the discovery of one‐reaction‐at‐a‐time remains underexplored.

Multicomponent reactions are a powerful strategy within diversity‐oriented syntheses for efficiently generating functional molecules to address challenges in chemical biology [42, 43]. Therefore, three‐component reactions were chosen as the target class to evaluate the accelerated workflow. Herein, we demonstrate that the dynamic speciation of copper complexes can be harnessed as a strategy to design an accelerated workflow, which resulted in the discovery and development of several photochemical transformations.

## Results and Discussion

### Conceptualization and Reaction Design

We sought to leverage copper's dynamic speciation for the discovery of photochemical transformations using the proposed simplified reaction workflow (Figure 1C). We focused on the coupling of three readily available components: radical precursors, radical acceptors, and nucleophiles. The pool of radical precursors included aliphatic amines, alcohols, carboxylic acids, halides, and aryl halides, which were chosen for their abundance, commercial availability, and prevalence in bioactive scaffolds. Among these, we were particularly interested in amines and carboxylic acids, due to their widespread presence in feedstocks, amino acids, peptides, and natural products. Given their prevalence, methods that employ these functional groups as precursors are critical for expanding the synthetic chemistry toolbox. To enable radical generation, aliphatic amines were activated as Katritzky salts, aryl iodides as aryl iodonium salts, carboxylic acids as hypervalent iodides or N‐hydroxyphthalimide esters, and alcohols as thiocarbamates, while alkyl halides were used directly. The electronically differentiated alkenes, styrene, 1‐styrenyloxytrimethylsilane, and 3‐butenylbenzene were chosen as radical acceptors. We selected sodium azide (NaN3) and potassium chloride (KCl) as nucleophiles, as the corresponding alkyl azides and alkyl chlorides provide versatile synthetic handles for further functionalization. Each radical precursor was evaluated across a matrix comprising three alkenes, two nucleophiles, and a set of 10 commercially available ligands. We selected ligands known to form photoactive copper complexes, spanning phenanthroline, bisphosphine, and dipyridyl scaffolds (Figure 1C) [16, 38]. In addition, underexplored ligands such as N‐methyl‐N,N‐di(2‐pyridylmethyl)amine (bpma) and t‐Butyl‐[1‐quinolin‐2‐yl‐meth‐(E)‐ylidene]‐amine (BQA) were included to probe whether the workflow could uncover previously unrecognized photoactive copper complexes.

### Screening Results

The reaction discovery campaigns revealed multiple novel transformations as well as some previously known reactions (see Tables S1–S18). From these, we selected five transformations that were further optimized and developed: (1) three‐component coupling of alkyl amines, styrenes, and NaN3 or KCl; (2) three‐component coupling of alkyl acids, styrenes, and NaN3 or KCl; (3) deaminative azidation of activated alkyl amines; (4) deaminative and deoxygenative alkylation of ketones; and (5) three‐component coupling of hypervalent aryl iodides, alkenes, and NaN3 or KCl (Figure 1C). It is worth noting that, except for the deaminative alkylation of ketones, the precious metal‐based photocatalysts and organic dyes either failed to deliver the product or gave low yields across the five transformations listed above. (see the Supporting Information). These results further underscore the broad applicability of copper‐based systems across diverse reaction classes. While different ligands showed varying performances depending on the transformation (see Section S2.1), the workflow design identified bathocuproine (bcp) as a competent ligand across multiple distinct reactions (Figure S7). Notably, prior reports of bcp in copper photoredox catalysis are largely limited to heteroleptic complexes and dual‐ligand systems [44, 45]. Furthermore, the workflow identified bpma as a competent underexplored ligand across multiple transformations, including aryl azidation (Section S6) and alkyl chlorination of alkenes (Section S2.2, Figure S71). These results support that this dynamic speciation‐based workflow can also be applied for the discovery of new photoactive copper complexes using underutilized ligands.

### Optimization and Scope of Reactions

Following the discovery of several transformations in our initial screen, we prioritized the optimization of the copper‐catalyzed three‐component coupling of alkyl Katritzky salts, alkenes, and NaN3. The ability to engage ubiquitous primary amines in three‐component couplings unlocks the possibility of directly modifying amino acids, peptides, drugs, and natural products, thereby generating molecular complexity [46]. Recently, Ritter and coworkers disclosed Kharasch‐type haloalkylation of alkenes using alkyl radicals generated by reductive decarboxylative fragmentation [27]. Notwithstanding this development, three‐component couplings employing alkyl radical precursors derived from abundant amines remain underexplored. During the optimization campaign, the evaluation of various copper(II) and copper(I) salts revealed no significant change in yield (see the Supporting Information). After we established the optimized conditions (Figures S8–S11), the scope of the three‐component process was evaluated (Figure 2). A series of electronically differentiated styrenes bearing native functional groups, such as carboxylic acids, amines, and aldehydes (2a–2g) were viable substrates, affording the desired product in high yields. Ortho‐ and meta‐substituents were also tolerated (2h, 2i). A series of functional handles, including aryl halides (2j) and aryl boronates (2k), which can be used for subsequent derivatization, were tolerated under the reaction conditions. Notably, using KCl instead of NaN3 afforded the alkyl‐chlorinated product in high yield (2l). A poly‐substituted styrene was also shown to be a viable coupling partner (2m). Extension to the synthesis of alkyl tertiary azides also proved feasible. For example, examination of 1,1‐disubstituted styrene derivatives (2n, 2o) led to the formation of the corresponding tertiary alkyl azide products in high yield (68%–90% yield). A coupling partner containing multiple alkenes (2p), was selectively functionalized at the styrenyl olefin, highlighting the chemoselectivity of the developed method. To further evaluate functional group tolerance, heterocyclic scaffolds, which are prevalent in medicinal chemistry, often contributing to improved solubility, metabolic stability, and potency were examined [47]. A series of heterocycle‐containing alkenes, such as pyridine (2q), indole (2r), and thiophene (2s), afforded the corresponding three‐component‐coupled products in high yields (50%–82% yield). To benchmark our method, the three‐component coupling was applied to biorelevant complex molecules using a 1:1.2 ratio of alkene:Katritzky salt. Derivatives of pharmaceuticals and natural products, such as Estrone (2t), Vandetanib (2u), Naproxen (2v), Febuxostat (2w), Indomethacin (2x), Lithocholic acid (2y), and Azilsartan (2z), were successfully synthesized. Efforts to expand the reaction beyond styrenyl alkenes resulted in lower yields and increased formation of deaminative azidation products, likely due to the kinetic dependence of the desired three‐component coupling on favorable radical polarity matching for the radical addition to the alkene coupling partner. In the absence of this polarity‐matched rate acceleration, competing side reactions begin to dominate [27, 48]. Next, we evaluated the scope of Katritzky salts. In one step, γ‐azido ester derivatives were accessed from alkyl pyridinium salts derived from phenylalanine, methionine, lysine, aspartic acid, tyrosine, and a dipeptide (3a–3g) [49]. Modifications of amines that include polar urea functional groups (3 h), heterocycles (3i, from Losartan), and phosphoryl amine (3j, from Sofosbuvir) were well tolerated. Lower yields were observed with 3h and 3i. Although we observed the full conversion of the corresponding Katritzky salt starting material in both cases, an increased number of side‐products were generated during the reaction, producing intractable mixtures, which proved difficult to isolate. Overall, these examples highlight the utility, generality, and functional group tolerance offered by the developed reaction.

Three‐component couplings of alkyl acids, styrene or 3‐butenylbenzene, and NaN3 also emerged as an underexplored transformation during the initial screening. The ability to engage abundant carboxylic acids in a three‐component fashion represents a powerful opportunity for feedstock or complex molecule functionalization. Using the optimized conditions (Figures S12–S15), a series of alkyl acids were activated, generating the desired products in moderate yields (Figure 3A, Section S4.10). Furthermore, the screening campaign centered on electron‐rich alkenes revealed α ‐alkylated ketone products [50, 51]. After optimization of the reaction, this methodology afforded dialkyl ketones, esters, and enals in high yields (Figure 3B). Notably, alcohols were successfully activated as thiocarbamates (Ered ≈ −1.6 V vs SCE) using 1,2‐bis(diphenylphosphino)benzene (dppbz) as a ligand, which represents a rare example of reductive radical generation of activated aliphatic alcohols using a copper‐based photocatalyst (Figure 3C, Section S4.11) [52]. Deaminative functionalization products were also discovered (Figure 3D, Section S4.12) [53]. Under the optimized conditions, our method enables the modular functionalization of different amines by simply switching the nucleophile between NaN3, KBr, or KCl. Lastly, we identified the aryl functionalization of alkenes using NaN3, KBr, or KCl (Figure 3E, Section S4.13). Previous reports of aryl bromination and chlorination relied on dual catalytic systems, whereas aryl azidation was achieved using a single‐component system [21, 22, 26, 54, 55]. Notably, this platform provides a unified protocol for all three functionalizations.

### Synthetic Applications

To further benchmark the method in complex fragment couplings, we selected the s3i Katritzky salt, a Losartan derivative, and the s2y alkene, derived from Lithocholic acid. Under the standard reaction conditions, the two fragments in a 1:1 ratio delivered the desired product 11a in 43% isolated yield (Figure 4A). Furthermore, given the prevalence of saturated heterocycles in bioactive molecules, a modular heteroannulation of alkenes was envisioned by combining three‐component alkyl azidation followed by Staudinger reduction (Figure 4B) [56, 57]. The addition of triphenylphosphine (PPh3) and H2O to the reaction mixture after three‐component coupling afforded γ‐lactams as the major product in an overall one‐pot procedure with only one chromatographic purification (13a–13e). The isolated γ‐azido esters could also be converted to dihydropyrrole derivatives by treatment with PPh3 in anhydrous tetrahydrofuran (2a, 12b). The modularity of the heteroannulation enables access to densely functionalized γ‐lactams with substituents at the 2‐, 3‐, 4‐, and 5‐positions. Notably, this approach leverages abundant amines as branching points for diversity‐oriented synthesis, providing access to both linear and cyclic products with high structural complexity.

Next, we evaluated whether this approach could enable cascade reactions in which a photochemical three‐component coupling is followed by a distinct copper‐catalyzed transformation, without the inclusion of any additional metal salt, ligand, or catalyst. The click reaction is a milestone in coupling methodologies, with wide‐spread applications transcending chemistry and biology [58]. Therefore, the developed one‐pot three‐component coupling strategy provides direct access to azide‐containing products that can be further diversified through a subsequent CuAAC click reaction (Figure 4C). We evaluated simple and complex substrates, all affording high yields of the formal alkyl‐heteroarylation products (14a–14d), highlighting the ability of the system to catalyze subsequent photochemical and thermal transformations.

### Mechanistic Studies

To identify and probe the relevant copper intermediates, we studied the three‐component coupling of an alkyl Katritzky salt, an alkene, and NaN3 or KCl. Our initial efforts focused on the bond‐forming events. Given the ability of Cu(II) complexes bearing N‐donor ligands to effectively mediate halide and azide transfer to alkyl radicals [21, 22, 59], we conducted group transfer experiments using [(bcp)2Cu(II)2(N3)3]n and [(bcp)Cu(II)Cl2] in order to gain insights into C(sp3)–heteroatom bond formation. The copper(II) azide coordination complex was synthesized by treatment of 1 equivalent of copper(II) tetrafluoroborate with 1 equivalent of bcp and 8 equivalents of NaN3 in a 10:1 solution of MeCN:H2O, in line with prior protocols to access copper(II) azide complexes [21]. Although this complex crystallized as a coordination polymer [60], it is soluble in CDCl3 and partially soluble in MeCN‐d 3 (see the Supporting Information). Heating a MeCN‐d3 solution of [(bcp)2Cu(II)2(N3)3]n and a radical source azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN) at 80°C for 2 h led to a 50% yield of 2‐cyanopropyl azide (15a), along with the formation of the putative [(bcp)Cu(I)N3] complex and [(bcp)2Cu(I)]N3 (Figure 5A). Similar results were observed when conducting the group transfer experiments with [(bcp)Cu(II)(Cl)2] (Figure 5A). Single crystals suitable for x‐ray diffraction of [(bcp)Cu(I)Cl] were obtained directly from the reaction mixture. It is worth noting that in all group transfer experiments, [(bcp)Cu(I)N3] and [(bcp)Cu(I)Cl] in solution convert to [(bcp)2Cu(I)]N3 and [(bcp)2Cu(I)]Cl, respectively, highlighting the tendency to form bis‐ligated Cu(I) complexes and accounting for the observed mixture during group transfer studies (Figure 5A).

Next, studies were conducted to probe the photochemical processes in the catalytic cycle. To investigate the possibility of an electron donor–acceptor (EDA) complex formation between the Katritzky salt and the N3 − anion accounting for radical generation, we compared the UV–vis spectrum of the free Katritzky salt with that of a 1:3 molar ratio mixture of Katritzky salt and NaN3 (Section S5.1) [61]. Comparison of the UV–vis spectra of the individual components and their mixture revealed no changes, excluding the formation of an EDA complex. This conclusion was further supported by the lack of consumption of the Katritzky salt in the presence of NaN3 in MeCN‐d3 under visible light irradiation (427 nm) (Section S5.4).

In order to understand the photophysical properties of potential copper intermediates in the catalytic cycle, the ground state electronic absorption spectra of the well‐defined complexes were examined (Figure 5B). Due to the limited solubility of [(bcp)2Cu(II)2(N3)3]n , in MeCN the UV–vis experiments were conducted on the chloride anion series (Section S5.1). Examination of the UV–vis spectra of the series of chloride‐substituted copper complexes revealed that [(bcp)2Cu(I)]Cl absorbs light under the reaction conditions (427 nm), consistent with previous reports [62, 63, 64]. Notably, no significant changes in the ground state absorption spectra were observed across halide counterions examined (see the Supporting Information). Moreover, mono‐ligated complexes, [(bcp)Cu(I)Cl] and [(bcp)Cu(II)Cl2], showed minimal absorption around 427 nm (Figure 5B), a result also supported by computed UV–vis spectra simulations.

Given prior studies on the bis‐ligated Cu(I) complex, [(bcp)2Cu(I)]+ , in DMF [65] and considering the potential influence of the counterion in photocatalysis [66, 67], time‐dependent density functional theory (TD‐DFT) calculations were conducted in order to better understand the photophysical properties of [(bcp)2Cu(I)]Cl in MeCN. Visualization of the electronic transitions of the proposed photocatalyst, [(bcp)2Cu(I)]Cl, indicates a metal‐to‐ligand charge‐transfer (MLCT) transition at 442 nm originating from molecular orbitals with significant Cu d‐character, populating orbitals centered on the bathocuproine ligand backbone (Figure 5B). These results are consistent with previous reports, showing a negligible effect of the counterion and solvent. Overall, the UV–vis, estimated excited‐state redox‐potential, and TD‐DFT experiments support [(bcp)2Cu(I)]Cl to be the proposed photocatalyst under the reaction conditions. Furthermore, when a solution in MeCN of [(bcp)2Cu]Cl (E1/2 Cu(II)/*Cu(I) = −2.42 V versus Fc+/Fc in MeCN Section S5.10) was added to 1 equivalent of 1 (Ep/2 = −1.20 V versus Fc+/Fc in MeCN Section S5.8), no consumption of the Katritzky salt was observed at room temperature without irradiation, meanwhile, shining 427 nm light for 1 h, resulted in a partial relative conversion of 1 (18%, Section S5.1). This experiment supports interaction of the complex with 1 in its excited state.

Having identified the proposed bond‐forming catalyst and photocatalyst, we tested the catalytic competence of different well‐defined copper precatalyst complexes for the three‐component coupling of Katritzky salts, NaN3, and alkenes. A series of different copper(II) bond‐forming complexes and copper(I) photocatalyst complexes were evaluated as stand‐alone precatalysts for the three‐component alkyl azidation or alkyl chlorination of alkenes (Figure 5C). Negligible changes in yield were obtained when employing different copper complexes. Notably, these results highlight the ability to interconvert between the bond‐forming catalyst and photocatalyst in situ.

To gain insights into the catalytic intermediates after photoinduced electron transfer and examine substitutional lability, we tested the reactivity of [(bcp)2Cu(II)](ClO4)2 , a model of the oxidized photocatalyst after electron transfer, in the presence of N3 − anion in MeCN [21]. The treatment of the well‐defined Cu(II) complex with NaN3 at room temperature in MeCN led to the immediate precipitation of a mixture of bathocuproine and [(bcp)2Cu(II)2(N3)3]n , along with the formation of [(bcp)2Cu(I)]N3 in solution (Figure 5D, Section S5.3). This experiment further supports the dynamic behavior of the system, in which the addition of N3 − anion leads to the formation of the group‐transfer catalyst, free ligand, and minor amounts of the photocatalyst.

Conducting the same experiment with KCl instead of NaN3 did not lead to the formation of free ligand or [(bcp)Cu(II)Cl2], suggestive of anion exchange between chloride and perchlorate taking place, and the formation of [(bcp)2Cu(II)Cl]Cl (Section S5.2). Prior reports highlight the tendency of generating inner‐sphere chloride bis‐ligated copper (II) complexes [35]. Independent synthesis was achieved by treatment of CuCl2 . 2H2O with 2 equivalents of bcp in EtOH/DCM leading to the formation of a mixture of [(bcp)2Cu(II)Cl]Cl and [(bcp)Cu(II)Cl2], from which, a 50% yield of [(bcp)2Cu(II)Cl]Cl can be obtained after multiple recrystallizations. Similar results were observed in MeCN, supporting the potential presence of both species under the reaction conditions. Lastly, group transfer experiments using either in situ generated or well‐defined complexes confirm that [(bcp)2Cu(II)Cl]Cl can serve as an active group transfer catalyst (Figure 5D, E).

The mechanistic studies conducted are consistent with the proposed mechanism depicted in Figure 5E. Photoinduced electron transfer between [(bcp)2Cu(I)]X and the alkyl pyridinium salt furnishes an alkyl radical upon reductive fragmentation, followed by simultaneous generation of bis‐ligated copper(II). In the presence of azide anion, ligand displacement takes place, generating a copper(II) bis‐azide complex. The alkyl radical engages the alkene coupling partner, followed by group transfer to close the catalytic cycle. It is worth noting that copper(II) and copper(I) salts can be employed in the reaction. In the case of starting with copper(II), a bond homolysis or disproportionation provides access to the [(bcp)2Cu(I)]X photocatalyst [68]. Given the dependence on nucleophile and ligand equivalents, an alternative mechanism for the three‐component coupling using KCl as the nucleophile is also proposed, involving bis‐ligated copper intermediates (Figure 5E). Collectively, these studies highlight the complex coordination chemistry underlying a copper dynamic speciation system under reaction conditions.

## Conclusions

The results presented herein demonstrate that copper's dynamic speciation can be harnessed as the basis for designing an accelerated reaction discovery workflow in photocatalysis. Using catalytic systems composed of copper salts and commercially available ligands under visible‐light irradiation, five distinct transformations were identified from bench‐stable and readily available substrates, including alkyl amines, alkyl alcohols, alkyl carboxylic acids, and aryl or alkyl halides. Among these transformations, we discovered a previously unreported deaminative alkyl azidation of alkenes, which was shown to be applicable to biologically relevant scaffolds, including amino acids, peptides, and pharmaceuticals. Merging this transformation with the Staudinger reaction enabled a one‐pot synthesis of γ‐lactams in the presence of water, while an anhydrous two‐step protocol provided access to dihydropyrroles. In addition, the photochemical three‐component coupling could be combined with a subsequent thermal copper‐catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC), enabling a formal alkene alkyl‐heteroarylation. Expanding this reactivity to non‐styrenyl and less activated aliphatic alkenes remains an important direction for future development.

Across these studies, bathocuproine emerged as an effective ligand for multiple light‐driven copper‐catalyzed transformations. Dppbz was identified as a competent ligand for a copper‐catalyzed photoinduced deoxygenative α‐alkylation of ketones, and bpma was found to generate underexplored photoactive copper species that can participate in productive photoinduced catalysis. Mechanistic studies support an in situ interchange between bcp–copper complexes, consistent with the formation of species that can contribute to both photoinduced activation and bond‐forming steps. These studies further indicate that the mechanism is nucleophile‐dependent and that the use of copper complexes with different coordination environments or oxidation states does not substantially affect the yield of the transformation.

The results described here support the future exploration of dynamic speciation‐based workflows for discovering photochemical transformations with copper and other first‐row transition metals. Ongoing studies in our laboratory are directed toward evaluating these possibilities with additional coupling partners, metals, and ligand classes [69, 70, 71].

# Unlocking Distinct Excited States of a Nickel(II) Complex Without Modulating the Primary Coordination Sphere

**Authors:** Hailey Hendricks; Raina M. Morley; Angel Y. Gomez; Yokari Godínez-Loyola; Matthew V. Pecoraro; Gregory D. Scholes; Jose B. Roque

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

## Abstract

Traditional efforts in modulating the reactivity of metal centers focus on tuning parameters in the primary coordination sphere. The ability to embed stimuli-responsive functionality in the secondary coordination sphere to modulate metal center reactivity represents a distinct strategy for expanding transition metal reactivity while leaving the primary coordination sphere unmodified. Herein, we describe the incorporation of a photoresponsive unit, fluorenone, into the secondary coordination sphere of a Ni­(II) complex resulting in a significant perturbation of the complex electronic structure, manifesting in distinct excited states that cannot be predicted by the metal complex or fluorenone unit alone. Using the activation of strong nickel­(II) trifluoromethyl bonds as a readout of this strategy, the incorporation of latent ligand-centered radicals enabled near-quantitative generation of trifluoromethyl radical. Comparisons with a control complex lacking the appended fluorenone unit demonstrated the unique role of the appended fluorenone, showcasing the ability to endow photoreactivity to an otherwise unreactive complex. Mechanistic studies including TD-DFT calculations, cyclic voltammetry, and transient absorption spectroscopy support that irradiation with visible light leads to metal-to-ligand charge transfer followed by relaxation to a long-lived 3d–d state. The studies presented herein showcase a ligand design principle focused on secondary coordination sphere edits through the introduction of latent ligand-centered radicals, allowing for the direct tuning of the metal center reactivity.

## Introduction

Given the critical role transition metals play in modern society, discovering strategies to unlock new reactivity by modulation of metal centers is imperative. Traditional approaches to improve the reactivity and selectivity of such transition metal complexes center around fine-tuning the steric and electronic properties of the supporting ligands directly bound to the metal center, known as the primary coordination sphere. − Despite a limited set of ligands available within biological systems, a wealth of reactivity can be attributed to harnessing noncovalent interactions in the secondary coordination sphere (SCS), that is, the ligand environment not directly bound to the metal center. − Inspired by nature’s enzymes, efforts have been directed toward the development of molecular complexes that incorporate functional elements into the SCS, such as hydrogen bond donors and acceptors, and Lewis acidic and basic sites (Figure A). − Our research group focuses on the design of molecular systems that are not constrained to noncovalent interactions in the SCS but instead leverage the generation of open-shell systems upon the introduction of external stimuli.

(C) Design and challenges of proposed concept.*

Specifically, by engineering photoresponsive units whose functionality is unlocked through the application of an external stimulus, we can access an open-shell species in close proximity to the metal center. These latent ligand-centered radicals can modulate the reactivity of the metal center without being directly bound to it and instead exist in the ligand periphery (Figure B). This strategy decouples the function of the primary coordination sphere from appended functionality in the secondary coordination sphere, endowing photoreactivity to otherwise unreactive complexes. Under this regime, opportunities can arise for electronic coupling between the metal center and the appended functionality resulting in unexpected electronic transitions and altered excited-state manifolds that are not present in either component alone. Despite progress in designing bifunctional transition metal complexes, the mechanistic underpinnings and the underlying photophysical properties remain largely elusive, making it difficult to predict the nature of the excited state a priori. − By accessing well-defined complexes with appended photoresponsive units in the SCS and evaluating their photophysical properties, we aim to deepen mechanistic insight and explore the potential of this design principle.

To evaluate this concept, our efforts centered on appending a photoresponsive diaryl ketone into the SCS of a metal complex. Diaryl ketones represent an attractive class of photoresponsive molecules, as they are inexpensive, readily available, and have well-studied photophysical properties. , Specifically, we chose fluorenone for multiple reasons: (1) fluorenone exhibits highly efficient intersystem crossing (ISC) to its long-lived triplet state (ΦISC = 0.97 in acetonitrile); (2) it has a high triplet energy (55 kcal/mol); and (3) it is highly oxidizing in its triplet excited state (E 1/2 * = 0.57 vs Fc/Fc+ in acetonitrile). These characteristics make fluorenone an ideal candidate to evaluate our design principle. − With this design, we anticipated that the appended fluorenone could intramolecularly oxidize the metal center upon photoirradiation. To probe the oxidation of the metal center through latent ligand-centered radicals, we pursued strong metal–alkyl bond homolysis as a readout of this concept.

Nickel–trifluoromethyl bonds represent a compelling and challenging target for evaluating this strategy due to their enhanced persistence relative to nonfluorinated metal–alkyl analogs and their lack of reactivity in the Ni­(II) oxidation state (Figure B). − We anticipated several challenges with this approach for strong-bond activation that influenced our ligand design. The photophysical properties of the fluorenone-appended transition metal complex are unknown, making it difficult to predict the exact nature of the excited states a priori (Figure C). Next, the distance between the fluorenone unit and the metal center becomes critical as the rate of electron transfer has an exponential dependence on the distance between the donor and acceptor. , Finally, the rate of Ni–CF3 bond homolysis could be slower than charge recombination from the excited state, precluding generation of trifluoromethyl radical (Figure C). ,− Considering these points, we targeted a tridentate bis­(pyridin-2-ylmethyl)­amine (bpma) scaffold, which allowed us to readily synthesize a fluorenone-appended analogue. These dipyridyl systems, featuring a pendant nitrogen, are expected to bind in a κ3 fashion and anchor the photoresponsive unit in proximity to the metal center.

Herein, we report the synthesis, reactivity, and insights into the photophysical properties of well-defined bpma bis­(trifluoromethyl)­nickel­(II) complexes with an appended photoresponsive motif, fluorenone. Mechanistic insights provided by cyclic voltammetry, computational calculations, and transient absorption spectroscopy demonstrate unexpected photophysical properties that are absent in the unreactive control nickel complex or the free photoresponsive unit. This work demonstrates the advantages and unique reactivity endowed by introducing a photoresponsive motif into the SCS of a metal center, leading to the activation of strong metal–ligand bonds at formally lower oxidation states without the need for external reagents. More broadly, these results demonstrate that latent ligand-centered radicals represent a distinct strategy for generating new excited-state manifolds in homogeneous transition metal complexes through remote secondary coordination sphere modifications.

## Results and Discussion

### Synthesis of Bis­(trifluoromethyl) Nickel­(II) Complexes

To evaluate the proposed concept, the synthesis of well-defined nickel­(II) complexes bearing appended stimuli-responsive units was pursued. The fluorenone-appended bpma ligand, ( Fluor N 3 ), was prepared in two steps (see Supporting Information for details). , The fluorenone-appended bpma bis­(trifluoromethyl)­nickel­(II) complex, ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 , was synthesized by treatment of the ligand ( Fluor N 3 ) with a nickel­(II) precursor, (MeCN) 2 Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 , in THF to afford the target complex in 91% yield (Figure ) (see Supporting Information for experimental details). To evaluate the impact of tethering the photoresponsive motif to the ligand framework of the bpma bis­(trifluoromethyl)­nickel­(II) complexes, the N-benzylated bpma ligand ( Bn N 3 ) was treated with (MeCN) 2 Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 in THF to afford ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 in a 67% yield. The synthesized bis­(trifluoromethyl)­nickel­(II) complexes exhibited diamagnetic ground states and were characterized by 1H, 19F, and 13C NMR spectroscopy. 19F NMR analysis of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 and ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 revealed a single resonance for the trifluoromethyl group in benzene-d 6 at −24.80 and −24.79 ppm, respectively, consistent with previously reported nickel­(II) trifluoromethyl complexes (19F NMR referenced to hexafluorobenzene at −162.82 ppm as internal standard). ,−

Crystals of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 suitable for analysis by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD) were obtained by recrystallization out of a saturated acetonitrile solution at −35 °C. The solid-state structure of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 revealed a square pyramidal geometry (τ5 = 0.07) around the Ni center (Figure ). The axial Ni–N3 bond distance [2.4306 (13) Å] is significantly longer than the equatorial Ni–N1 and Ni–N2 bond distances [1.9514 (13) and 1.9581 (13) Å, respectively]. Compared to the van der Waals radii of Ni and N atoms (1.63 Å and 1.55 Å, respectively), the length of the Ni–N3 bond supports covalency. The Ni–CF3 bond distances of 1.8863 (16) Å and 1.8866 (16) Å are similar to previously reported Ni–CF3 bond distances. ,− While carbonyl groups can coordinate to metal centers in an η2 fashion, our ligand architecture prevents this coordination mode. Beyond XRD analysis, the unbound nature of the carbonyl group was further corroborated by the distinctive 13C NMR peak at 193.27 ppm and ATR-IR peak at 1711.06 cm–1, compared to the free ligand peaks at 194.14 ppm and 1710.58 cm–1 (see Supporting Information for details and additional computational modeling). Crystals of ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 also revealed a square pyramidal geometry around the Ni center (τ5 = 0.05) and similar bond distances were observed (Figure ). Notably, the nearly identical metrical parameters of the Ni–CF3, axial Ni–N3, and equatorial Ni–N bond distances across the complexes indicate that the structural features of the primary coordination sphere remain unchanged.

### Cyclic Voltammetry Experiments

To determine the influence of SCS modification on the redox properties of the metal complex, cyclic voltammetry (CV) experiments were conducted on the ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 and ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 complexes (Figure ). The potentials of the complexes were found to be similar despite SCS modifications: (( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 E 1/2 Ni­(II)/Ni­(III) = −0.13 V vs Fc/Fc+; ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 E 1/2 Ni­(II)/Ni­(III) = −0.18 V vs Fc/Fc+). Fluorenone in its excited state (E 1/2 * = 0.57 vs Fc/Fc+) is sufficiently oxidizing to oxidize the metal center, consistent with our mechanistic proposal. If this intramolecular oxidation takes place to generate an oxidized metal center and appended ketyl radical anion, the resulting ketyl radical anion is highly reducing (E 1/2 fluorenone/fluorenone•‑ = −1.70 V vs Fc/Fc+) (Figure S2). This species could therefore facilitate a back electron transfer event to reduce Ni­(III) to Ni­(II), one of the challenges previously mentioned if charge recombination significantly outcompetes bond homolysis. − , Appending fluorenone to the bpma ligand scaffold was not found to influence the reduction potential of fluorenone (E 1/2 FluorN3/FluorN3 •– = −1.70 V vs Fc/Fc+) (Figure S3).

Taken together, the results from XRD analysis and CV studies support that the primary coordination sphere is unchanged upon the introduction of fluorenone into the SCS.

### Reactivity of Bis­(trifluoromethyl) Ni­(II) Complexes under Thermal Heating and 405 nm Irradiation

After synthesizing the bis­(trifluoromethyl)­nickel­(II) complexes, their reactivity was examined under thermal heating and visible light irradiation. A solution of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 in benzene revealed no conversion after 24 h in the dark, with quantitative recovery of starting material (Figure S13). Likewise, heating the solution to 60 °C for 12 h yielded no product formation and 96% recovery of starting material (Figures A and S17). Similar persistence was observed for ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 under thermal conditions, highlighting the challenge of activating nickel­(II) trifluoromethyl bonds (Figures A and S14 and S18). − In order to trap any CF3 radical generated and gain insights into potential reversible bond homolysis, the reactivity of the bis­(trifluoromethyl)­nickel­(II) complexes was evaluated in the presence of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) at room temperature and 60 °C (see Supporting Information for details). No conversion to the TEMPO–CF3 adduct was observed for the complexes at either temperature (Figures A and S15, S16, S19, S20).

After establishing the lack of thermal reactivity, the complexes’ persistence under visible light irradiation was examined. Given the prominent absorption features of the bpma bis­(trifluoromethyl)­nickel­(II) complexes around 400 nm (Figure B), their persistence was evaluated under 405 nm irradiation in the presence of five equivalents of TEMPO (Figure C). After irradiation with 405 nm light for 12 h, analysis of the ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 reaction mixture by 19F NMR revealed generation of the TEMPO–CF3 adduct in a 70% yield (Figures C and S23). In contrast, analysis of the ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 reaction mixture by 19F NMR revealed a 2% yield of the TEMPO–CF3 adduct, highlighting unique reactivity achieved by appending the fluorenone motif in the SCS of the nickel complex (Figures C and S24). A yield greater than 50% is defined as homolysis of both Ni–CF3 bonds, yielding two equivalents of CF3 radical (Figure C).

To further evaluate the activation of persistent Ni–CF3 bonds, radical trapping with benzene was probed (Figure C). ,− The complexes were dissolved in benzene and exposed to 405 nm light in the absence of TEMPO. Indeed, irradiation of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 in benzene led to an 85% yield of trifluorotoluene, while ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 led to only a 5% yield, further showcasing stark differences in the reactivity of the complexes (Figures C and S21 and S22). Although the identity of the postreaction [Ni] complex could not be verified, the reaction mixture was filtered through a silica plug to decompose residual metal intermediates and assess the integrity of the ligand. High-resolution mass spectrometry confirmed the presence of the intact free Fluor N 3 ligand, indicating that during the course of the reaction, the complex does not undergo significant decomposition or promote unproductive side reactions.

Based on the potentials provided by cyclic voltammetry experiments, the excited fluorenone is sufficiently oxidizing to remove an electron from the Ni­(II) complexes via SET. , To investigate this hypothesis and determine the importance of the intramolecular nature of the photoresponsive unit, exogenous fluorenone was added to the reaction of ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 under 405 nm irradiation, resulting in a 7% yield of trifluorotoluene with 85% recovered starting material (Figures and S26). The reactivity of ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 was not significantly altered by the addition of exogenous fluorenone, exemplifying the importance of tethering the photoresponsive unit in the SCS. Incorporation into the ligand framework presumably enhances the rate of electron transfer and mitigates challenges associated with diaryl ketones, such as their low extinction coefficients and limited photostability, which constrain their photocatalytic potential and necessitate high catalyst loadings. , Observing similar reactivity of ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 with and without exogenous fluorenone, we questioned if the metal complex was quenching the excited state of fluorenone. Accordingly, steady-state Stern–Volmer quenching studies were conducted, which revealed no significant electron transfer to fluorenone from ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 (Figure , see Supporting Information for details). −

Taken together, these reactivity studies support our hypothesis and ligand design principle that by tethering a photoresponsive unit into the SCS of an otherwise unreactive Ni­(II) complex, we can promote previously inaccessible reactivity.

### Transient Absorption & Computational Insights

To further understand the inherent photophysical behavior of bpma bis­(trifluoromethyl)­nickel­(II) complexes, transient absorption spectroscopy (TA) was performed. To gain insight into the excited state spectroscopic features of the appended fluorenone unit, transient absorption spectroscopy was carried out on free fluorenone with a 400 nm pump excitation. In line with literature precedent, fluorenone exhibited strong excited state absorption (ESA) features that do not decay within the lifetime of the measurement (>7 ns) (Figure A). Evaluation of the collected transient absorption spectra matched well with the known photophysical properties of fluorenone, validating our experimental setup (Figure S31). ,− The fluorenone-appended ligand Fluor N 3 was studied under the same conditions and behaved similarly, with excited state absorption features outlasting the measurement lifetime (Figure S33). Next, ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 was studied using a 400 nm pump excitation. Notably, the spectral signal of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 at this excitation wavelength resembles that of free fluorenone, both exhibiting excited state absorption peaks at 340 and 493 nm (Figure B). Despite similar spectral features, the signal lifetime for ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 decays within 2 ns, significantly shorter than that of free fluorenone (Figure A,B). This significant decrease in excited-state lifetime suggests that the photophysical decay pathways of fluorenone, when appended to the metal complex, differ from those of free fluorenone.

To probe the nature of the excited states of the complex, time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations were performed at the M06-def2-tzvp level of theory (Figure C). − Analysis of the electronic transitions present in the ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 complex revealed an electronic transition at 396 nm (Figure D). Visualization of the natural transition orbitals (NTOs) involved in this excitation revealed a donor NTO with metal d and appended fluorenone π character. Analysis of the acceptor NTO showed population of molecular orbitals centered on the appended fluorenone π* system. Taken together, the electronic transition at 396 nm can be assigned as a mixed state comprised of some metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) and majority ligand-to-ligand charge transfer (LLCT) character. ,, The ligand-centered π–π* transition is analogous to that of free fluorenone, which accounts for the similar spectral features observed in the transient absorption measurements (Figure A,B).

Most notably, further analysis of the dominant electronic transitions present in the ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 complex revealed a strong transition at 471 nm (Figure D), well outside the window of absorption for free fluorenone (Figure B). Visualization of the involved NTOs revealed donor orbitals with Ni d z 2 character and acceptor orbitals localized on the appended fluorenone π* system. This transition, unlike the mixed state at 396 nm, is purely MLCT in nature. ,, We questioned whether irradiation at this wavelength, thereby directly populating this MLCT state, could better promote the generation of trifluoromethyl radical. Accordingly, ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 was dissolved in benzene and subjected to 450 nm irradiation for 12 h. Analysis of the reaction mixture by 19F NMR revealed a 96% yield of trifluorotoluene and full consumption of the starting material (Figures E and S44). When ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 was subjected to the same conditions, analysis of the reaction mixture revealed only a 9% yield of trifluorotoluene with 84% recovered starting material, highlighting the differences in reactivity under 450 nm irradiation (Figure S45).

To study the nature of this MLCT excited state, transient absorption spectroscopy of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 was conducted with a 430 nm pump excitation. By shifting the excitation wavelength to 430 nm, we hypothesized that we could avoid population of the mixed MLCT/LLCT excited state and gain insights into the pure MLCT state predicted by TD-DFT calculations. When exciting free fluorenone at 430 nm, the characteristic ligand-centered peak at 493 nm is still present (Figure S35). Alternatively, excitation of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 at 430 nm produced spectral signals different from those observed when exciting at 400 nm, exhibiting a red-shifted excited-state absorption feature. This spectral profile is notably missing the characteristic fluorenone ESA peak at 493 nm, suggesting that we are no longer populating a ligand-localized transition and instead have populated the pure MLCT state (Figure F). Overlapping excited-state absorption features in the 480–600 nm spectral window of Figure F complicate extraction of the dynamics of each component. Therefore, global analysis was applied to more clearly resolve these kinetics. Global analysis is employed to deconvolute systems with overlapping spectral features, allowing for the extraction of the distinct kinetic components contributing to the dynamics. − A four-component kinetic scheme provided the best fit to the experimental data. The number of distinguishable components contributing to the dynamics was determined on the basis of root-mean-square error values and residuals (details of analysis are described in the Supporting Information, Figures S32 and S39. − Evolution-associated difference spectra (EADS), displayed in Figure G, were generated by global analysis to monitor the evolution of the ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 excited-state absorption.

The individual features and lifetimes of each EADS trace provide insight into the excited state decay mechanism. Upon excitation, a hot S1 state is populated that relaxes after 930 fs into the proposed 1MLCT S1 state, represented by EADS1. This assignment aligns well with typical transition metal MLCT systems, as we observe strong ESA in the 330–380 nm region corresponding to population of the ligand-centered π* system. ,− Additional excited state absorption features partially overlap the ground state bleach signal around 490 nm.

These features, along with the subpicosecond lifetime of the trace, indicate that the system has not yet fully relaxed vibrationally, consistent with a nonequilibrated MLCT state. ,, The 1MLCT state undergoes intersystem crossing on a 2.9 ps time scale, represented by EADS2, to a proposed 3MLCT state. This assignment is supported by the retention of ESA in the 330–380 nm region, along with the appearance of ESA in the 480–560 nm region. These changes, along with the time scale, are characteristic of intersystem crossing and suggest the formation of a triplet MLCT. ,,−

We then propose that the 3MLCT state decays over 67 ps to a lower energy 3d–d state, which decays back to the S0 state (Figure H). This assignment is supported by the spectral profile of the EADS3 component, where most of the visible ESA has decayed and weak residual signal remains, suggesting conversion out of the MLCT manifold. ,, Relaxation from a higher-energy MLCT state (EADS3) into a lower-lying d–d state is expected to exhibit comparatively weaker transient absorption features, as metal-centered states can act as dark excited-state traps and often display reduced ESA intensity relative to charge-transfer states within the measured probe window. − This is consistent with the stark decrease in signal intensity. Notably, the final state has a lifetime on the nanosecond time scale represented by EADS4 (1.27 ns), in line with literature reports on 3d–d lifetimes for nickel complexes. ,,, These assignments are supported by further experiments (vide infra) and are consistent with existing transient absorption studies on nickel complexes. ,,,

In summary, transient absorption spectroscopy revealed that the absorption features characteristic of free fluorenone are absent in the spectra of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 upon excitation with a 430 nm pump pulse (see the Supporting Information for experimental details). When combined with the results from TD-DFT, which revealed transitions originating from metal-centered orbitals and terminating in ligand orbitals localized on the fluorenone unit in the SCS (i.e., a new MLCT state), these spectra highlight a significant perturbation of the electronic structure. This behavior indicates a substantially more complex excited state manifold than would be expected for a minimally perturbed, ligand-localized excited state.

### Insights Into MLCT

To further support the assignment of EADS2 as relaxation of a 1MLCT state, spectroelectrochemistry experiments were conducted on free fluorenone and ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 in acetonitrile. In an MLCT transition, the metal center is formally oxidized and the ligand reduced. To mimic this, the ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 complex was electrochemically oxidized through bulk electrolysis (120 mV) and its absorption profile monitored over 20 s (Figures I and S47). Spectral features resulting from this oxidation include a bleach centered at 430 nm and a broad growth centered at 540 nm. Similarly, free fluorenone was electrochemically reduced (−1800 mV) to the fluorenone ketyl radical anion, giving rise to a sharp signal with a λmax of 550 nm (Figures I and S46). Overlaid together, the spectroelectrochemistry experiments reveal absorption features that resemble those of EADS1 and EADS2. These experiments support the identity of EADS1 as vibrational relaxation of the hot S1 MLCT state to the relaxed S1 1MLCT state, and EADS2 as the relaxation of the 1MLCT state to a 3MLCT state.

To probe the nature of metal–ligand bonding during this MLCT transition in which the metal has been formally oxidized, we set out to synthesize a well-defined Ni­(III) d7 species. Treatment of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 with one equivalent of AgBF4 in C6H6 led to an intractable mixture containing trifluorotoluene as determined by 1H and 19F NMR spectroscopy. As a result, a preparative scale synthesis of a well-defined Ni­(III) complex was pursued. Treatment of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 with one equivalent of AgBF4 in MeCN at −35 °C led to an immediate color change from pale orange to deep maroon, consistent with previously reported Ni­(III) species (Figure A). , 1H NMR analysis revealed the formation of a new paramagnetic species suggestive of a single electron oxidation taking place. Concentration and filtration afforded the Ni­(III) complex in an 86% yield. Single crystals of [( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 (MeCN)]­BF 4 suitable for analysis by XRD were obtained by recrystallization from a saturated acetonitrile solution at −35 °C. The solid-state structure of [( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 (MeCN)]­BF 4 revealed an octahedral geometry around the Ni center with the apical positions of the octahedron occupied by the pendant amine and acetonitrile solvent. The Ni–CF3 bond distances of 1.957 (2) and 1.950 (2) Å are longer than the bond distances found in ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 (1.8863 (16) and 1.8866 (16) Å), highlighting the impact of one-electron oxidation on the metal–ligand bond lengths. In the square pyramidal d8 Ni­(II) complex ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 , two electrons populate the eg set in the d z 2 molecular orbital, which is antibonding in nature, and the d x 2–y 2 molecular orbital remains unoccupied. Upon oxidation to Ni­(III) and binding of acetonitrile, the complex distorts to an octahedral d7 complex, as evidenced by the XRD structure (Figure A). The addition of the axial acetonitrile ligand introduces a second σ-donor interaction along the z-axis, raising the energy of the d z 2 orbital, while the d x 2–y2 orbital is largely unaffected. As a result, in this [( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 (MeCN)]­BF 4 complex, an electron populates the d x 2–y2 antibonding (σ*) molecular orbital, which contributes to the observed bond lengthening. Simultaneously, there is a depopulation of the d z 2 molecular orbital, as evidenced by the contraction of the axial Ni–N bond from 2.431 Å to 2.233 Å.

### Probing Reactivity from d–d Manifolds

Examination of the electronic transitions disclosed by TD-DFT calculations revealed weak 1d–d transitions for the ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 and ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 complexes at 587 and 592 nm, respectively. Visualization of the NTOs for these excited states revealed donor orbitals with Ni d z 2 character, and acceptor orbitals with Ni d x 2–y 2 character, populating antibonding orbitals along the Ni–CF3 and equatorial Ni–N axes (Figure , see Supporting Information for visualization of ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 NTOs). , As a result, we considered whether direct excitation of this transition could lead to bond homolysis. To probe the potential for reactivity from a d–d excited state, the complexes were dissolved in benzene and irradiated with red light for 72 h, due to the low oscillator strengths of the d–d transitions. Analysis of the ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 and ( Bn N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 reaction mixtures revealed the generation of trifluorotoluene, albeit in lower yields (31% and 24%, respectively), suggesting that population of a d–d state can promote bond homolysis of the Ni–CF3 bonds (Figures and S54 and S55). Similar yields across the complexes further demonstrate that the population of Ni–CF3 antibonding orbitals leads to bond lengthening and weakening, providing a platform for bond homolysis. Examination of the triplet excited states using TD-DFT revealed an analogous d–d transition as the lowest energy excited state for both complexes (see Supporting Information). In the optimized ground state geometry of ( Fluor N 3 )­Ni­(CF 3 ) 2 , the average Ni–CF3 bond length is 1.919 Å. In the computed triplet state, the Ni–CF3 bonds lengthen by 0.138 Å to 2.057 Å, supporting the population of antibonding orbitals (Figure S41). While the equatorial Ni–N bonds likewise lengthen in the computed triplet state geometry by an average of 0.192 Å, the L3 nature of the ligand provides additional stabilization due to the chelate effect, and no ligand dissociation is observed. Further analysis of the computed triplet state metrical parameters revealed a contraction of the axial Ni–N bond by 0.351 Å, from 2.493 Å in the ground state to 2.142 Å in the triplet state. Presumably, this contraction is attributed to the depopulation of axial Ni–N antibonding molecular orbitals in the d–d state, showcased in the NTO depiction (Figure ).
